hints: Look closely at how the carbon skeleton and functional group change from propan-1-ol to each product.
Remember that propan-1-ol to propene loses $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, which is the classic test for dehydration.
Check the other rows for impossible reaction types, like addition to a saturated alcohol or complete combustion giving only carbon monoxide.
walkthrough:
**Start from propan-1-ol**

Think of propan-1-ol as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, a saturated primary alcohol. It can be substituted, oxidised, dehydrated or burned, but it cannot undergo addition because it has no $\text{C=C}$ double bond.

Structure:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Match each product to its real reaction type**

1-chloropropane forms by substitution of $\text{OH}$ by $\text{Cl}$, propanal forms by oxidation (loss of hydrogen), and complete combustion must give $\text{CO}_2$, not $\text{CO}$.

Key dehydration equation:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Pick the only fully correct row**

Only propene from loss of water is correctly described as dehydration of propan-1-ol. The other rows pair a real product with the wrong reaction name.

options.A: Incorrect. Propan-1-ol to 1-chloropropane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, is possible with $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{SOCl}_2$, but it is substitution (nucleophilic substitution) of $\text{OH}$ by $\text{Cl}$, not addition. Addition requires a $\text{C=C}$ bond, which propan-1-ol does not have.
options.B: Incorrect. Complete combustion of any hydrocarbon or alcohol in excess oxygen gives carbon dioxide plus water, $\text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. Carbon monoxide is the product of incomplete combustion, so the reaction type and product do not match.
options.C: Correct. Heating propan-1-ol with concentrated sulfuric acid or passing over hot $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ removes $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to form propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$. This loss of water from an alcohol to form an alkene is exactly dehydration (an elimination reaction).
options.D: Incorrect. Propan-1-ol to propanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, is possible, but it is oxidation (using acidified $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ with distillation), not reduction. Oxidation removes hydrogen from the alcohol carbon, while reduction would add hydrogen.
